A model to mini-quench early galaxies by balancing stellar feedback and gas accretion

Judah Luberto Email: judah@astro.ucla.edu    and Steven R. Furlanetto Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of California,
475 Portola Plaza, Los Angeles, CA, USA Email: sfurlane@astro.ucla.edu
Abstract

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered a population of low-mass, early galaxies with very low levels of star formation over tens of Myr. These “mini-quenched” galaxies were one of the many surprises from JWST and still require a robust explanation. We seek to explain a few important properties of these galaxies, namely the timescales governing their star formation and quenching. We use a simple model that pairs stellar feedback with the forces binding gas to a z∼6z\sim 6 galaxy, and with plausible parameter choices, this model produces mini-quenching in galaxies approximately as large as observed mini-quenched galaxies – up to total stellar masses of ∼1010​M⊙\sim 10^{10}M_{\odot}. In our model, the ejected interstellar gas forms into a spherical shell that expands outward during quenching. Our novel improvement is allowing this expanding shell to prevent accreting gas from falling in, in contrast to other models whose shells do not interact with accreting gas. Using our model, if a galaxy accretes isotropically, we find that stellar feedback can reproduce observed timescales of mini-quenching with plausible galaxy-formation parameter values. However, at low halo masses, the quenching timescale of our model is too long (>100>100 Myr). A potential solution for a long quenching time is for the galaxy to accrete via filaments, in which case only a portion of the shell interacts with the accreting gas and the quenching timescale decreases to more accepted values. However, the ram pressure from feedback cannot stop filaments with very small opening angles, as occur in some halo formation models, making mini-quenching impossible. Finally, we use this model to estimate the fraction of galaxies undergoing mini-quenching, finding that it can be large.

Keywords
high-redshift galaxies, galaxy formation

1 Introduction

Analytic models and simulations predict that when a young galaxy grows during Cosmic Dawn, it will fluctuate between periods of higher and lower rates of star formation Stinson et al. (2007); Merlin et al. (2012); Faucher-Giguère (2018); Orr et al. (2019). To gain intuition for why this stochasticity might occur, let us consider a simple argument of timescales: the star formation timescale is tied to the dynamical timescale, which controls the speed at which gas can collapse and form dense clouds. These timescales are ∝(1+z)−3/2\propto(1+z)^{-3/2}, and at early epochs the star-formation timescale becomes less than or comparable to the feedback timescales from those stars (a few tens of Myr for supernova). Short star-formation timescales mean early galaxies could form multiple generations of stars at higher rates before feedback could prevent further star formation, leading to higher net star formation efficiencies. The detailed implications of this trend depend on the details of star formation inside galaxies. With a simple galaxy formation model, Furlanetto and Mirocha (2022) found that stochastic star formation could occur in low mass galaxies (mh≲1011​M⊙m_{h}\lesssim 10^{11}M_{\odot}), while Dekel et al. (2023) argued that it could occur primarily in massive galaxies (the “feedback-free” model).

While some (simple) models of this stochasticity included phases where the accumulated feedback halted all star formation, these episodes were generally assumed to be oversimplifications. However, recent observations have found a population of early (z≳3z\gtrsim 3) and low-mass (m∗,tot<1010​M⊙m_{*,\rm tot}<10^{10}M_{\odot}11 1 Note that we define observed/total stellar mass as m∗,totm_{*,\rm tot} instead of the more common m∗m_{*}. This is because we later denote m∗m_{*} as the stellar mass produced since the beginning of a single star-formation episode in our model.) galaxies with zero star formation. The constant number densities of these galaxies across z∼4z\sim 4–66 suggests their star formation is episodic and not permanent Yang et al. (2025); Merlin et al. (2025) (leading many to call these galaxies “mini-quenched”). This mini-quenching occurs over a broad range of galaxy masses. For example, across the varied types of observations (e.g., photometric color cuts Valentino et al. (2023); Alberts et al. (2024), photometric fitting Merlin et al. (2025), spectroscopic observations Marchesini et al. (2023); Strait et al. (2023); Looser et al. (2024); Covelo-Paz et al. (2026), and spatially-resolved lensed systems Hutchison et al. (2025); Messa et al. (2025)), many of these galaxies have stellar masses up to m∗,tot∼109m_{*,\rm tot}\sim 10^{9}–1010​M⊙10^{10}M_{\odot}, likely corresponding to relatively large halo masses mh∼1011m_{h}\sim 10^{11}–1012​M⊙10^{12}M_{\odot}. Apparently, we should put effort into understanding how this mini-quenching occurs and what requirements it places on models.

The driving mechanism behind this population of mini-quenched galaxies very likely differs from typical quenched galaxies at lower redshifts. Locally, at around m∗,tot∼1010​M⊙m_{*,\rm tot}\sim 10^{10}M_{\odot}, most galaxies transition from the blue type to the red type Martis et al. (2016), suggesting that late quenching is associated with a mass transition, in contrast to the broad range in which it is seen at high redshifts. Second, at late times quenching persists over very long timescales (≳1\gtrsim 1–22 Gyr), whereas mini-quenched galaxies do not form stars on the order of a few tens of Myr. Because the latter is much smaller than the age of the Universe even during the Cosmic Dawn, mini-quenching appears to be a temporary phenomenon, unlike normal quenching.

Moreover, the internal and external quenching mechanisms common to local galaxies are as follows (though our summary is brief and the interested reader should see De Lucia et al. (2025a) for a review). Internally, high-mass galaxies can host active galactic nuclei (AGN). Accretion onto a central black hole can release enough energy to create massive outflows in high-mass galaxies Silk and Rees (1998); Choi et al. (2015) or provide enough heating to prevent star formation in these galaxies Somerville et al. (2008). Also internally, galaxies could be quenched by their morphological features (e.g., Martig et al. (2009)). High-mass (m∗,tot>1010​M⊙m_{*,\rm tot}>10^{10}M_{\odot}) early galaxies might be quenched by similar processes to local galaxies Carnall et al. (2023a); Russell et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025), as large AGN appear in some early quenched galaxies Carnall et al. (2023b); Baker et al. (2025b); Stevenson et al. (2025), and they could even affect star formation in the surrounding environment Zhu et al. (2025). But signatures of AGN are much harder to observe in low-mass galaxies Hegde et al. (2024); Feltre et al. (2016); Gutkin et al. (2016); Sanders et al. (2023), even though some low-mass galaxies do appear to host large black holes (e.g., Harikane et al. (2023); Juodžbalis et al. (2025)).

Additionally, low-redshift galaxies can be quenched by their external environment. High-mass galaxies tend to live in denser environments, and interactions with the surrounding environment can cause quenching (e.g., Baldry et al. (2004); Balogh et al. (2017)). Massive early galaxies are found in a wide range of environments Binh et al. (2025); De Lucia et al. (2025b); Singh et al. (2025), suggesting that environmental quenching mechanisms could be present in galaxies in the most dense environments. Some lower-mass mini-quenched galaxies have been found in overdense environments as well Alberts et al. (2024); Baker et al. (2025a); Witten et al. (2025), but there is no compelling evidence for an environmental cause.

Here we focus on a model in which stellar feedback ultimately causes mini-quenching. Previous analytic models so far have treated outflowing gas and inflowing gas as operating independently of each other (e.g., Davé et al. (2012); Dekel et al. (2013); Furlanetto and Mirocha (2022)). Even in models which track the location of a shell of outflowing gas, the shell is typically assumed not to affect accretion (e.g., Yamaguchi et al. (2023)). However, as long as the outflowing gas is incident on the inflowing gas, it is possible that these gases will counteract each others’ motion. Therefore, we create a model in which an outflowing thin shell prevents gas from accreting onto the galaxy, choking off the supply of gas for star formation. This approach should be seen in conjunction with previous attempts to model temporary quenching in early galaxies, either through analytic models (e.g., Gelli et al. (2024); Dekel et al. (2023)) or results from simulations (e.g., McClymont et al. (2025); Katz et al. (2025); Gelli et al. (2020); Dome et al. (2024)).

The purpose of this paper is to present a model which can reproduce important observables of early mini-quenched galaxies using stellar feedback prescriptions. In section 2, we present our galaxy source model. Within this section, we include an implementation of gas accretion by filaments and the motion of the gas leaving the galaxy. In section 3, we use this model to calculate an approximate maximum halo mass that may be mini-quenched. In section 4, we compare our model to a few key observables of mini-quenched galaxies. In section 5, we discuss extensions of our model and implications of mini-quenching in general, and in section 6, we offer the conclusions of our results.

Unless otherwise specified, throughout this work we use a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology with Ωm=0.3111\Omega_{m}=0.3111, ΩΛ=0.6889\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.6889, Ωb=0.0489\Omega_{b}=0.0489, h=0.6766h=0.6766, consistent with the results of Planck Collaboration et al. (2020).

2 A model of feedback from a source galaxy

The purpose of this section is to present our model of mini-quenching in early galaxies, in which stellar feedback removes gas from a galaxy and prevents further gas from accreting onto its inner star-forming region.22 2 We focus on mechanical effects rather than gas heating (e.g., Gelli et al. (2024)) because of fast cooling timescales at early times (scaling as ∝∼(1+z)−3\mathrel{\vbox{\halign{\hfil$#$\cr\propto\cr\kern 2.0pt\cr\sim\cr\kern-2.0pt\cr}}}(1+z)^{-3}). The process of quenching a single galaxy in our model is as follows:

  1. 1.

    A low-mass, early galaxy has just completed a previous mini-quenched cycle and begins to accrete gas onto its inner region. We assume the gas depleted from the previous mini-quenching period is recycled back onto the galaxy so that the gas mass is proportional to the halo mass: mg=(Ωb/Ωm)​mhm_{g}=(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h}.

  2. 2.

    The galaxy forms stars out of the gas in its reservoir. Given that this galaxy was previously quenched, only the newly-created stars produce feedback.

  3. 3.

    Meanwhile, the galaxy accretes gas, either isotropically or along filaments. The gas accretion adds to the gas reservoir and may be used to form stars until the galaxy is quenched.

  4. 4.

    The gas reservoir in the galaxy is pushed outwards by stellar feedback and pulled inwards by the halo’s gravitational force and the inward momentum of the accreted gas. We model the gas reservoir as a thin shell at the edge of the star-forming region to test whether feedback can overcome the inward forces and drive the gas outward.

  5. 5.

    Once the shell begins to move outward, the galaxy is considered quenched because there is no gas inside the galaxy. We label this the star-formation timescale, tSFt_{\rm SF}. The galaxy stops forming stars, though feedback continues. The forces on the shell cause the shell to move outwards, which we track using a shell motion equation.

  6. 6.

    As the shell expands, feedback eventually fades (because star formation has stopped), but the accreting gas continues to provide inward momentum to the shell. Our model assumes that the galaxy remains quenched until the shell falls back onto the galaxy. We label this the quenching timescale, tquencht_{\rm quench}.

In the following subsections, we describe the components of this picture in detail.

2.1 The halo potential well

The first step in creating a galaxy is to consider the halo in which the galaxy lives. In the standard theory of galaxy formation, all galaxies form in dark matter halos. For simplicity, we describe the halos as isothermal spheres whose mass profile is

mh​(r)=2​σ2​rG,m_{h}(r)=\frac{2\sigma^{2}r}{G}, (1)

where σ\sigma is the velocity dispersion of the halo. The velocity dispersion is the virial/circular velocity at the virial radius, rvirr_{\rm vir}:

σ2​(rvir)≈G​mhrvir.\sigma^{2}(r_{\rm vir})\approx\frac{Gm_{h}}{r_{\rm vir}}. (2)

The viral radius is defined as

rvir​(z)=[(200​GΔh​Ωm​mh)1/2​110​H​(z)]2/3∼3​kpc​(1+z7)−1​(mh108​M⊙)1/3,\begin{split}r_{\rm vir}(z)&=\left[\left(\frac{200G}{\Delta_{h}\Omega_{m}}m_{h}\right)^{1/2}\frac{1}{10H(z)}\right]^{2/3}\\ &\sim 3\mathrm{kpc}\left(\frac{1+z}{7}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot{}}}\right)^{1/3},\end{split} (3)

where Δh≡200\Delta_{h}\equiv 200 is the overdensity of a halo and H⁡(z)H(z) is the Hubble constant across redshift.

2.2 A simple galaxy growth model

Our model will trace the interaction of feedback with accreting gas, so we require a prescription for the latter. To begin, we initialize our galaxy to have a gas reservoir with mass mg=(Ωb/Ωm)​mhm_{g}=(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h} available for star formation. Using the framework and notation from Furlanetto et al. (2017), a dark matter halo which has a mass mhm_{h} grows approximately at a rate

m˙h=A​mh​(1+z)5/2,\dot{m}_{h}=Am_{h}(1+z)^{5/2}, (4)

where A=0.03/GyrA=0.03/\rm Gyr, which is the average growth rate of halos from Dekel et al. (2013). The baryons accrete at a rate (Ωb/Ωm)​m˙h(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})\dot{m}_{h}, so the gas reservoir grows as

m˙g=ΩbΩm​m˙h−m˙∗,\dot{m}_{g}=\frac{\Omega_{b}}{\Omega_{m}}\dot{m}_{h}-\dot{m}_{*}, (5)

where m˙∗\dot{m}_{*} is the instantaneous star-formation rate in the galaxy. The gas enters the galaxy with an inflow velocity equal to the virial velocity of the halo, σ\sigma, as supported by simulations Dekel et al. (2009); Goerdt and Ceverino (2015).

We parameterize the star-formation rate by a star-formation efficiency (SFE) per free-fall time, f∗f_{*}, such that

m˙∗=f∗tff​mg,\dot{m}_{*}=\frac{f_{*}}{t_{\rm ff}}m_{g}, (6)

where tfft_{\rm ff} is the free-fall time of the gas within the region of star formation. For consistency with previous results (e.g., Faucher-Giguère (2018); Furlanetto and Mirocha (2022)), we use the free-fall time of a disk galaxy. We follow the scaling relations from Faucher-Giguère (2018) for the free-fall time, which calculates it at the half-mass radius of a disk inside a NFW halo (e.g., Navarro et al. (1996)). The free-fall time is tff≈0.2​torb≈0.0026/H⁡(z)t_{\rm ff}\approx 0.2t_{\rm orb}\approx 0.0026/H(z), where torbt_{\rm orb} is the orbital frequency of the disk.

As for the SFE, the value of f∗f_{*} for individual galaxies is unknown in (early) galaxy formation, though there is an approximate expected range of f∗∼[0.001,0.1]f_{*}\sim[0.001,0.1] that is commonly used (e.g., Furlanetto and Mirocha (2022)), with f∗=0.015f_{*}=0.015 being the standard local theoretical value Salim et al. (2015); Krumholz et al. (2018). Note that the instantaneous SFE is different than the time-averaged SFE, f~∗=m∗,tot/mg\tilde{f}_{*}=m_{*,\rm tot}/m_{g}, which is the ratio of the total mass of stars (including stars formed before the initialization of our model; an observed quantity) and the gas mass.

We also require the dust mass, mDm_{\rm D}, in our model. We assume, again for simplicity, that D/D⊙=Z/Z⊙D/D_{\odot}=Z/Z_{\odot}, where D=mD/mgD=m_{\rm D}/m_{g}, D⊙=1/162D_{\odot}=1/162, and ZZ is the metallicity in the galaxy. Our fiducial value for the metallicity is Z/Z⊙=10−4Z/Z_{\odot}=10^{-4}, which is representative of extremely pristine gas (often associated with Population III star formation), though we will find in section 3.2 that the forces directly associated with metallicity are subdominant (a metallicity of Z/Z⊙=0.1Z/Z_{\odot}=0.1 changes our results by ∼1%\sim 1\%).

2.3 Galaxy radius

We parameterize the radius of the galaxy as R0​(t)=κ​rvir​(t)R_{0}(t)=\kappa r_{\rm vir}(t). If a galaxy has a rotationally-supported disk, the edge of the star-forming region would have κ≈0.035\kappa\approx 0.035, the typical spin parameter of the disk Mo et al. (2010). This is the smallest extent our galaxies can have.

Early galaxies can form stars in a much larger region because they may have not formed well-defined disks at this point (e.g., Danhaive et al. (2025)). Sun et al. (2026) created a framework of star formation in a turbulent circumgalactic medium and found that stars can form out to κ∼0.4\kappa\sim 0.4–0.50.5, though at much smaller rates than will be formed at smaller radii. We approximate the numbers of stars forming at κ>0.4\kappa>0.4 as zero and set a maximum extent of κ=0.4\kappa=0.4.

Throughout the paper, we will use κ=0.035\kappa=0.035 as a fiducial choice. We will find that for isotropic accretion our choice of κ\kappa does not affect the results, although in section 3.4 we will see that it can affect the results when filamentary accretion is included.

2.4 Initial mass function

One of the more important assumptions in our model is the distribution of masses of stars in the galaxy. Because we focus on mini-quenching at early times, we allow our stellar population to follow a more “top-heavy” initial mass function (IMF), which is one whose stars exist at higher masses on average, perhaps motivated by its lower metallicity. Given the lack of constraints on the IMF at early times Glover and Klessen (2026), we choose to follow the flexible IMF functional form in Lazar and Bromm (2022), which expresses the number of stars per unit stellar mass as

Φ⁡(mstar)=d​Nd​mstar=M⊙A1​mstar−α​exp⁡[−(mcharmstar)β],\Phi(m_{\rm star})=\frac{dN}{dm_{\rm star}}=\frac{M_{\odot}}{A_{1}}m_{\rm star}^{-\alpha}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{m_{\rm char}}{m_{\rm star}}\right)^{\beta}\right], (7)

where A1A_{1} is a normalization constant (defined by OPEN∫mstar​Φ​d​mstar=1​M⊙)\int m_{\rm star}\Phi dm_{\rm star}=1M_{\odot}). We allow stars to form in a mass range mstar=0.08m_{\rm star}=0.08–100​M⊙100M_{\odot}. We choose β=1.6\beta=1.6 throughout the paper (aligning with, e.g., Wise et al. (2012); Jeon et al. (2015); Lazar and Bromm (2022)). The parameter β\beta represents the IMF shape at mstar<mcharm_{\rm star}<m_{\rm char}, which is of lesser importance in our model.

To highlight the flexibility of this functional form, we show in figure 1 how it can approximate the well-known Chabrier IMF Chabrier (2003) (solid black line). The dashed purple line uses the functional form of equation 7 with α=2.35\alpha=2.35, β=1.6\beta=1.6, and mchar=0.2​M⊙m_{\rm char}=0.2M_{\odot}. We call this set of parameter values a “Chabrier-like” IMF for the rest of the paper.

The IMF form in equation 7 is also flexible enough to create more top-heavy (or bottom-heavy) distributions than the Chabrier IMF. We visualize this effect in figure 1 for a number of α\alpha and mcharm_{\rm char} parameter combinations. Focusing first on the characteristic mass, we see that increasing the mcharm_{\rm char} value from the Chabrier-like value of 0.2​M⊙0.2M_{\odot} to 5​M⊙5M_{\odot} (dashed blue line), the IMF distribution shifts quickly toward higher masses.

For our model, the key implication of the IMF is how it affects the amount of stellar feedback, which is driven by massive stars. We might expect a more top-heavy IMF to always produce more feedback. However, more feedback in a stellar population is not a simple mapping to larger mcharm_{\rm char} values: because the average stellar mass increases with mcharm_{\rm char}, the number of stars decreases. It is possible to increase the average mass too much, such that the fraction of stars with masses >8​M⊙>8M_{\odot} increases, but the total number of supernovae decreases. To understand this complex interplay of parameters, we draw a vertical gray line denoting 8​M⊙8M_{\odot} in figure 1 (the minimum stellar mass which can go supernova). Because the IMF drops dramatically at higher star masses, the important quantity to focus on is the value of the IMF at and around 8​M⊙8M_{\odot}. Most of the supernovae will occur in this range. For α=1.35\alpha=1.35, we find that increasing mcharm_{\rm char} from 0.2​M⊙0.2M_{\odot} to 10​M⊙10M_{\odot} actually decreases the number of stars above >8​M⊙>8M_{\odot}.

Of the IMF parameter sets shown, [α=2.35\alpha=2.35, mchar=5​M⊙m_{\rm char}=5M_{\odot}] has the highest fraction of stars that will go supernova. For the rest of this paper, we will refer to this parameter set as our “top-heavy” IMF and use it to show how an IMF more top heavy than the Chabrier IMF will affect the mini-quenching process.

2.5 Stellar lifetimes

Because mini-quenching is a time-dependent process, we next need to determine the timescales over which newly-formed stars will drive feedback. We approximate the lifetime of a star as equal to its time on the main sequence. We follow the lead of Orr et al. (2019), who for simplicity find the stellar lifetimes using a mass-to-light scaling of Population I stars:

mstar(t)=(t1010​yrs)−2/5M⊙,m_{\rm star}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{10^{10}\rm yrs}\right)^{-2/5}M_{\odot}, (8)

which also produces produces similar lifetimes as low-metallicity, Population III populations (e.g., Schaerer (2002); Klessen and Glover (2023)). Because the smallest star in our model to go supernova is 8​M⊙8M_{\odot}, we define the lifetime of that star to be tSN=55t_{\rm SN}=55 Myr.

2.6 Radiative feedback from stars

We next need to determine how feedback from the galaxy’s stars drives gas outward (which we model as the force on a thin shell). To begin, we estimate the force produced on a shell from radiation pressure. Throughout this section, we refer the interested reader to Thompson and Heckman (2024) for a review.

2.6.1 UV-driven dusty winds

One effective source of radiation pressure is the UV emission of massive, hot stars: if the photons are absorbed by dust, and if the dust and the gas are dynamically coupled, the UV photons impart an outward momentum on the gas. We thus begin with the UV luminosity per stellar mass of a population of age t′t^{\prime}:

where x⁡(t′)x(t^{\prime}) is mass of a star with a lifetime t′t^{\prime} (the maximum star mass still alive after time t′t^{\prime}), L∗,UV​(m)=4​π2​R∗2​(m)​BUV​(m)L_{\rm*,UV}(m)=4\pi^{2}R_{*}^{2}(m)B_{\rm UV}(m) is the UV luminosity of a single star with mass mm, R∗R_{*} is the radius of a star of a given mass, and BUV​(m)B_{\rm UV}(m) is the Planck function. But it will turn out that the force from UV-driven winds is sub-dominant even with the full UV wavelength range (100100–40004000Å), so we choose to use the entire range for simplicity. With these choices, our model produces about half the number of hydrogen-ionizing photons as a similar prescription with starburst99 Leitherer et al. (1999); the main difference is our choice of a Chabrier-like IMF. Our simple top-heavy IMF produces ∼20%\sim 20\% more ionizing photons than starburst99. The details of the stellar modeling thus affect our results modestly, with a comparable effect to the IMF choice.
