2.6.2 Lyα\alpha-driven winds

Early galaxies have less dust and their gas reservoirs are denser, creating conditions where Lyα\alpha radiation pressure can be the dominant force from stellar winds. After an ionizing photon is absorbed by the wind, Lyα\alpha photons can scatter multiple times within the shell, imparting momentum at each scatter (see Nebrin et al. (2025) for an in-depth calculation of the physics of this process).

Similar to the results from Nebrin et al. (2025), the Lyα\alpha luminosity per stellar mass formed of age t′t^{\prime} is

lLy​α​(t′)=(1−fesc,LyC)​frec,Ly​α​Q˙LyC​ELy​α,l_{\rm Ly\alpha}(t^{\prime})=(1-f_{\rm esc,LyC})f_{\rm rec,Ly\alpha}\dot{Q}_{\rm LyC}E_{\rm Ly\alpha}, (12)

where fesc,LyCf_{\rm esc,LyC} is the escape fraction of Lyman continuum photons (chosen to be fesc,LyC=0.1f_{\rm esc,LyC}=0.1), frec,Ly​αf_{\rm rec,Ly\alpha} is the fraction of recombinations that produce a Lyα\alpha photon (chosen to be frec,Ly​α=2/3f_{\rm rec,Ly\alpha}=2/3), Q˙LyC\dot{Q}_{\rm LyC} is the rate of production of Lyman continuum photons per solar mass (calculated in the same manner as L∗,UVL_{*,\rm UV}, but adapted for this quantity), and ELy​αE_{\rm Ly\alpha} is the energy of a Lyα\alpha photon. The total Lyα\alpha luminosity is

LLy​α​(t)=∫0tm˙∗​(t′)​lLy​α​(t−t′)​d​t′.L_{\rm Ly\alpha}(t)=\int^{t}_{0}\dot{m}_{*}(t^{\prime})l_{\rm Ly\alpha}(t-t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}. (13)

The Lyα\alpha force is a function of the Lyα\alpha “force multiplier,” MF\mathrm{M}_{\rm F}, which reflects the additional force generated by multiple scatterings of each Lyα\alpha photon and depends on the hydrogen column density, the dust to gas ratio, and the temperature of the shell (see Nebrin et al. (2025)). We approximate the temperature of the shell by assuming half of the dust-driven and Lyα\alpha luminosity is deposited as thermal energy and that the gas is cooled by the cooling functions from Schure et al. (2009), assuming solar abundance, to a minimum temperature of 104​K10^{4}\rm\ K, below which the cooling times become very long. Our choice of a cooling function derived for higher metallicities predicts faster cooling than the expected lower metallicity population, which results in larger MF\rm M_{F} values, and therefore more force from Lyα\alpha photons. Even with these large MF\rm M_{F} values, we will find the Lyα\alpha forces to be subdominant. With these results in mind, the force from Lyα\alpha-driven winds is

FLy​α=MF​LLy​αc.F_{\rm Ly\alpha}=\mathrm{M}_{\rm F}\frac{L_{\rm Ly\alpha}}{c}. (14)

2.7 Feedback from supernovae

Because supernovae suddenly release an enormous amount of energy into the surrounding medium, we treat their feedback differently than the momentum injection from stellar radiation in our model. More specifically, we imagine that supernovae build up a region of hot gas that exerts an outward pressure force against a surrounding (thin) shell Tegmark et al. (1993); Furlanetto and Loeb (2003); Yamaguchi et al. (2023).

The rate of supernovae at a time tt is equal to the rate at which stars above the threshold mass 8​M⊙8\ M_{\odot} are dying. Given our approximation for the stellar lifetimes in equation 8, this can be written as

N˙SN​(t)=∫0tm˙⋆​(t′)M⊙​[Φ⁡(ms​t​a​r)​d​mstard​t′]t−t′​d​t′,\dot{N}_{\rm SN}(t)=\int^{t}_{0}{\frac{\dot{m}_{\star}(t^{\prime})}{M_{\odot}}}\left[\Phi(m_{star})\frac{dm_{\rm star}}{dt^{\prime}}\right]_{t-t^{\prime}}dt^{\prime}, (15)

where the term in square brackets is to be evaluated at the stellar mass whose lifetime is equal to the time interval between the time of a star’s formation (t′t^{\prime}) and the time at which the supernova rate is evaluated (tt). In appendix A, we analytically calculate N˙SN\dot{N}_{\rm SN} as a function of f∗f_{*}, mhm_{h}, and time of star formation.

Supernovae force the gas shell outwards by supplying energy to the hot gas interior to the shell. Following Tegmark et al. (1993), we compute the pressure pushing on the shell via

P˙=Lp2​π​r3−5​P​vr,\dot{P}=\frac{L_{\rm p}}{2\pi r^{3}}-5P\frac{v}{r}, (16)

where LpL_{\rm p} is the rate of change in energy of the hot gas and vv is the velocity of the shell; the last term accounts for the energy loss from P​d​VPdV work. The supernovae supply energy, but the hot gas also cools (primarily) by Compton cooling (see Yamaguchi et al. (2023) for a discussion on the different forms of cooling):

Lcomp=−2​π​r3​Ptcomp,L_{\rm comp}=-\frac{2\pi r^{3}P}{t_{\rm comp}}, (17)

where tcomp=1.2×108​yr​[(1+z)/10]−4t_{\rm comp}=1.2\times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{yr}[(1+z)/10]^{-4} is the Compton cooling time. The total luminosity from the hot gas is then Lp=LSN+LcompL_{\rm p}=L_{\rm SN}+L_{\rm comp}, with LSN=ϵk​N˙SN×1051​ergL_{\rm SN}=\epsilon_{k}\dot{N}_{\rm SN}\times 10^{51}\rm erg. Here, ϵk\epsilon_{k} is the fraction of supernova energy released into the wind. We set ϵk=1\epsilon_{k}=1, though we comment on how a change in ϵk\epsilon_{k} will change our results in a later section. Finally, the force from supernovae on a shell at radius rr is

FP=4​π​r2​P.F_{\rm P}=4\pi r^{2}P. (18)

2.8 Gas accretion

The key question for mini-quenching is whether this feedback can halt accretion, choking off the galaxy’s gas supply. We now consider how the gas accretes onto the galaxy.

In simple models of early galaxy formation, accretion is often assumed to be isotropic. However, there is support for filamentary accretion at these times: Mandelker et al. (2018) used the Colossus code Diemer and Kravtsov (2015); Diemer (2018) to estimate which halos should be fed by filaments as a function of redshift. Using a crude estimate that all halos above a 2σ\sigma overdensity at any redshift will be fed by filamentary structures, the model estimated that all z=6z=6 halos above a mass mh≳3×109​M⊙m_{h}\gtrsim 3\times 10^{9}M_{\odot} will be stream fed. According to this argument, most observed early galaxies are fed by filaments of some kind. However, the rapid growth of the nonlinear mass scale makes this expectation highly redshift dependent: at z∼3z\sim 3, their threshold corresponds to mh≳3×1011​M⊙m_{h}\gtrsim 3\times 10^{11}M_{\odot}. While the exact relation between galaxies being fed by streams and their mass/redshift is unknown, it is clear that special attention should be made to the possibility that observed mini-quenched galaxies are supplied cold gas via filaments. We therefore consider both models in which accretion occurs isotropically and those in which accretion occurs along narrow filaments.

In the latter case, we assume gas filaments subsist down to the star-forming region of the galaxy and are conical, such that the radius of the filament scales linearly with the distance from the center of the galaxy (the same as, e.g., Mandelker et al. (2018)). This assumption is supported by simulations which resolve gas filament accretion in galaxies (e.g., Dekel et al. (2009); van de Voort et al. (2011)). Ramsøy et al. (2021) found that the radius of gas filaments are a few tens of percent of the virial radius (at the virial radius) for a Milky Way-like progenitor across cosmic time. However, for a broader range of halos and filament properties supported by simulations (e.g., Danovich et al. (2012)), Mandelker et al. (2018) estimated that at Cosmic Dawn, roughly, the filament radius is ∼0.08​rvir\sim 0.08r_{\rm vir} when evaluated at the virial radius (corresponding to a covering fraction of only ∼0.005\sim 0.005). They performed this calculation using an analytic model which assumed cold gas streams are supported by rotation (as they found cold streams supported by zero rotation are inconsistent with cosmological simulations and observations).

As long as gas filaments are conical, the solid angle of a gas stream as observed from the central galaxy is constant with radius:

θfil=π​arctan2⁡(rfilrvir).\theta_{\rm fil}=\pi\arctan^{2}\left(\frac{r_{\rm fil}}{r_{\rm vir}}\right). (19)

With this value in mind, the total covering fraction is

fcover=Nfil​θfil4​π,f_{\rm cover}=\frac{N_{\rm fil}\theta_{\rm fil}}{4\pi}, (20)

where NfilN_{\rm fil} is the number of filaments and θfil\theta_{\rm fil} is the solid angle covered by each filament, assuming each filament is the same size. Many cosmological simulations find that galaxies which accrete by filaments do so with one large, primary stream that makes up ∼50%\sim 50\% of the accretion rate, and two smaller streams which make up the rest of the accretion rate (e.g., Danovich et al. (2012)), but our model ignores these differences. Therefore, we assume Nfil=3N_{\rm fil}=3 identical streams for our filamentary model (similar to Mandelker et al. (2018)).

2.9 Motion of the outflowing shell

To initialize the system, we assume that the galaxy’s gas reservoir is in a thin shell at R0R_{0}, the effective radius of the star-forming region (see section 2.3). However, for our purposes we only need follow the portion of the shell that is incident on the accreting gas, because it determines what actually prevents the gas from accreting. This has an initial mass msh,f=fcover​mgm_{\rm sh,f}=f_{\rm cover}m_{\rm g}. If the shell is outflowing, it gains mass as m˙sh,f=(Ωb/Ωm)​m˙h\dot{m}_{\rm sh,f}=(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})\dot{m}_{h}. Otherwise, the accreting gas gathers into the gas reservoir of the galaxy.

The motion of the outflowing gas shell (incident on the accreting gas) is described via a force equation. Similar equations have been discussed before, both for radiation pressure on dusty shells Thompson et al. (2015); Ferrara et al. (2025); Manzoni and Ferrara (2025); Nakazato and Ferrara (2025) and supernova-induced pressure Tegmark et al. (1993); Furlanetto and Loeb (2003); Yamaguchi et al. (2023). However, our equation below includes the impact of filaments with the covering fraction of accreting gas:

msh,f​d​vd​t=−G​mh​msh,fr2−m˙sh,f​(vfil+v)+(FUV+FLy​α+Fp)​fcover.m_{\rm sh,f}\frac{dv}{dt}=-\frac{Gm_{h}m_{\rm sh,f}}{r^{2}}-\dot{m}_{\rm sh,f}(v_{\rm fil}+v)+(F_{\rm UV}+F_{\rm Ly\alpha}+F_{\rm p})f_{\rm cover}. (21)

where vfil=σv_{\rm fil}=\sigma is the inward velocity of the accreting gas, which is set to be always positive. The behavior of the shell is that when vv is positive, the shell moves outwards and the galaxy is considered quenched. In the equation above, the forces FUVF_{\rm UV}, FLy​αF_{\rm Ly\alpha}, and FpF_{\rm p} all scale with fcoverf_{\rm cover} because it is the fraction of the total force from the galaxy that is incident on the portion of the shell pushing against accretion.

We have assumed the gas reservoir is a thin shell at R0R_{0}. Realistically, the gas reservoir will take time to evolve from its diffuse state in a galaxy into a thin shell outside the galaxy’s star forming region, but this provides a minimal criterion for an outflow and is reasonable given that low-mass galaxies appear to quench in a few Myr Gelli et al. (2023). Our parameter ϵk\epsilon_{k} can account for the supernova energy lost in driving the gas from its initial configuration into a shell. We also note that we do not allow the shell to sink to smaller radii to prevent the unphysical result that r→0r\rightarrow 0 when v<0v<0.

Figure 2 demonstrates the paths of shells for two example galaxies, both of which form stars with f∗=0.001f_{*}=0.001 (and fcover=1f_{\rm cover}=1). The span between the beginning of shell motion and the end is the quenching timescale, tquencht_{\rm quench}. We write above curly brackets the approximate quenching timescales of each model halo as a visualization of the process.

3 An estimate for the largest mini-quenched galaxy

In this section, we derive a simple criterion for the limiting halo mass that can undergo mini-quenching by determining the conditions under which outward feedback forces overcome the binding forces of gravity and gas accretion. We explicitly perform this calculation for galaxies at z∼6z\sim 6, as some of the relevant processes have complex redshift dependence. We show results for other redshifts as well. In later sections, we will see that this simplified estimate of the maximum halo mass matches the results of our full model rather well.

3.1 Which inward forces dominate?

To begin, we consider the two inward forces (gravity and accretion) and determine which is more significant. The force of gravity from an isothermal halo on a shell is

Fg,max​(R0)=2​G​mh​msh​fcoverR0​rvir=4.2×1032​erg/cm​(mh108​M⊙)4/3​(κ0.035)−1​(fcover1),\begin{split}F_{g,\rm max}(R_{0})&=\frac{2Gm_{h}m_{\rm sh}f_{\rm cover}}{R_{0}r_{\rm vir}}\\ &=4.2\times 10^{32}\mathrm{erg/cm}\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)^{4/3}\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.035}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\rm cover}}{1}\right),\end{split} (22)

where we have assumed the mass of the shell is equal to the baryonic mass in an average galaxy, msh∼(Ωb/Ωm)​mhm_{\rm sh}\sim(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h}. The gravitational force depends on the halo mass, which increases throughout the period of star formation; according to equation 4, it will grow by a factor ξ=exp⁡[A​(1+z)5/2​tSF]\xi=\exp[A(1+z)^{5/2}t_{\rm SF}] . At z=6z=6, this factor can reach ≈1.5\approx 1.5 for tSF=100t_{\rm SF}=100 Myr, so we take ξ=1.25\xi=1.25 as a representative value and increase the effective gravitational force by a factor 1.254/31.25^{4/3} following the above mass scaling.

The second inward force is that from gas accreting onto the galaxy, for which

Facc=vacc​m˙g∼vvir​m˙h​(Ωb/Ωm)=2.9×1031​erg/cm​(mh108​M⊙)4/3,\begin{split}F_{\rm acc}&=v_{\rm acc}\dot{m}_{g}\\ &\sim v_{\rm vir}\dot{m}_{h}(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})\\ &=2.9\times 10^{31}\mathrm{erg/cm}\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)^{4/3},\end{split} (23)

where we have also multiplied the prefactor by ξ4/3\xi^{4/3}. The ratio of these two forces is

f1=Fg,maxFacc=9.3​(κ0.035)−1​(fcover1),f_{1}=\frac{F_{g,\rm max}}{F_{\rm acc}}=9.3\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.035}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\rm cover}}{1}\right), (24)

which means that the force of gravity is dominant if κ<0.32\kappa<0.32 (and fcover=1f_{\rm cover}=1). Because the maximum extent of our disk is κ≲0.4\kappa\lesssim 0.4, we assume below that the force of gravity exceeds the accretion force (for isotropic systems, although section 3.4 shows that this may not be true for filamentary accretion).

3.2 Which outward forces dominate?

While it has been found that the Lyα\alpha force is the dominant feedback force in the context of radiation pressure on low-metallicity gas Thompson and Heckman (2024); Nebrin et al. (2025), in our model, supernova pressure is dominant on the scales of the galaxy star-forming region.

In figure 3, we plot the fraction that each feedback mechanism contributes to the total outward force of two example galaxies. The ratio of each feedback force to the total force does not depend on f∗f_{*} because each force scales linearly with the SFE. However, the ratio does depend on how long each of these galaxies form stars, as shown on the xx-axis. For a very low-mass galaxy (left panel), the galaxy is dominated by supernova pressure after a few Myr of star formation. However, for a larger halo (right panel), the Lyα\alpha force can be strong up to ∼10\sim 10 Myr. This result suggests that stellar winds might be useful in creating the shell and causing mini-quenching on timescales of a few Myr (similar to the results of Gelli et al. (2024)), but supernovae are required to maintain quenching for longer timescales.

To find an analytic expression for the force from supernovae, we assume Compton cooling is subdominant, which (if OPENf∗∼0.01)f_{*}\sim 0.01) agrees with our full equations within ∼10%\sim 10\% (see appendix B). Then, equation 16 becomes Pmax=NSN​(tSF)​ESN/2​π​R03P_{\rm max}=N_{\rm SN}(t_{\rm SF})E_{\rm SN}/2\pi R_{0}^{3}, where NSN​(tSF)N_{\rm SN}(t_{\rm SF}) is the number of supernovae after a period of star formation. With an expression for NSN​(tSF)N_{\rm SN}(t_{\rm SF}) from appendix A, the maximum pressure force from supernova is

Pmax\displaystyle P_{\rm max} = 7.7×10−8​erg/cm3​(f∗0.01)​(κ0.035)−3\displaystyle=\ 7.7\times 10^{-8}\mathrm{erg/cm^{3}}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.035}\right)^{-3} (25)
×{(tSF/tSN)1.54if ​tSF≤tSN(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1if ​tSF>tSN.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{1.54}&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ (t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN}.\end{cases} (26)

where tchar=36t_{\rm char}=36 Myr and tSN=55t_{\rm SN}=55 Myr. As with the inward forces, this expression depends on the halo mass, which will evolve through the star formation episode. The pressure force scales as ∝NSN/rvir\propto N_{\rm SN}/r_{\rm vir}. For NSNN_{\rm SN}, we have used equation 51, which depends on mass. However, it suffices to use the initial halo mass because most of the supernova progenitors launching the wind must have formed in the early phases. Note that the virial radius scales as ∝ξ1/3\propto\xi^{1/3}, so we have included a factor ≈1.25−1/3\approx 1.25^{-1/3}. Now, relating the pressure of the hot gas to a force on the shell, the maximum force from the supernovae is

Fp,max\displaystyle F_{p,\rm max} = 9.7×1034​erg/cm⁡(f∗0.01)​(κ0.035)−1​(mh108​M⊙)2/3​(fcover1)\displaystyle=\ 9.7\times 10^{34}\mathrm{erg/cm}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.035}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)^{2/3}\left(\frac{f_{\rm cover}}{1}\right) (27)
×{(tSF/tSN)1.54if ​tSF≤tSN(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1if ​tSF>tSN.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{1.54}&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ (t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN}.\end{cases} (28)

3.3 The mini-quenching mass limit

We expect there to be a maximum halo mass in our model because Fp∝mh2/3F_{p}\propto m_{h}^{2/3} and Fg∝mh4/3F_{g}\propto m_{h}^{4/3}. To calculate this maximum halo mass, we begin by taking the ratio of the inward and outward forces:

Fp,maxFg\displaystyle\frac{F_{p,\rm max}}{F_{g}} = 270(f∗0.01)(mh108​M⊙)−2/3\displaystyle=\ 270\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)^{-2/3} (29)
×{(tSF/tSN)1.54if ​tSF≤tSN(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1if ​tSF>tSN.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{1.54}&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ (t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN}.\end{cases} (30)

Quenching can no longer occur when the inward forces are greater than the outward forces on the shell which occurs at a maximum halo mass:

mh,max\displaystyle m_{h,\rm max} =5×108​M⊙​(NSN1000)3/5\displaystyle=5\times 10^{8}M_{\odot}\left(\frac{N_{\rm SN}}{1000}\right)^{3/5} (31)
=4.4×1011​M⊙​(f∗0.01)3/2\displaystyle=4.4\times 10^{11}M_{\odot}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)^{3/2} (32)
×{(tSF/tSN)2.31,if ​tSF≤tSN[(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1]3/2,if ​tSF>tSN.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{2.31},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ [(t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1]^{3/2},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN}.\end{cases} (33)

One interesting result is that as long as the force of gravity is the dominant binding force (κ≲0.4\kappa\lesssim 0.4 at z=6z=6), the maximum halo mass is not a function of the extent of the star forming region. This is not an obvious result because a more extended galaxy exists on average in a lower gravitational potential, so its gas should be easier to kick from the system. But at the same time, a larger extent of gas increases the volume that supernova must heat up to achieve a similar pressure. These two effects cancel one another in the parameter range we consider, and mh,maxm_{h,\rm max} does not depend on κ\kappa.

A second (unsurprising) result is that this maximum halo mass value depends sensitively on the length of star formation. In short bursts of star formation, doubling the length of star formation allows for mini-quenching in halos five times larger!

In figure 4, we show how some key parameters affect mh,maxm_{h,\rm max} in this two-force model. Here, we no longer rely on scaling relations for the virial radius (equation 3) or the number of supernovae (equation 51), but solve these values numerically. In each panel of the figure, we display the maximum halo mass for f∗=0.01f_{*}=0.01 as a function of the star-formation timescale for several redshifts in which mini-quenched galaxies are observed. We plot the Chabrier-like IMF results as red lines and the representative “top-heavy” IMF as blue lines. While we would expect that a more top-heavy IMF would be more rare at z=3z=3 than, for example, z=9z=9, we plot these results in all panels for completeness.

We compare the numerical estimate to the analytic result in the z=6z=6 panel, where we show the latter with the black dotted line. Note the agreement at tSF∼55t_{\rm SF}\sim 55 Myr, which occurs because of our choice of the ξ\xi parameter; the estimate departs from the numerical results at larger times.

To convert a maximum halo mass to a maximum stellar mass value, we assume that mb=(Ωb/Ωm)​mhm_{b}=(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h} and scale the baryon mass to a stellar mass by a time-averaged star formation efficiency f~∗=m∗,tot/mb\tilde{f}_{*}=m_{*,\rm tot}/m_{b}. With these conversions, we find

m∗,tot,max\displaystyle m_{*,\rm tot,max} =6.9×109​M⊙​(f∗0.01)3/2​(f~∗0.1)\displaystyle=6.9\times 10^{9}M_{\odot}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{\tilde{f}_{*}}{0.1}\right) (34)
×{(tSF/tSN)2.31,if ​tSF≤tSN[(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1]3/2,if ​tSF>tSN.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{2.31},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ [(t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1]^{3/2},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN}.\end{cases} (35)

This implies that, with isotropic accretion and typical feedback parameters, it is reasonable to expect mini-quenching in moderately large galaxies. For very efficient star formation, mini-quenching could extend to much higher masses.

3.4 Inclusion of filaments in the approximation

Naively, we might not expect the inclusion of filaments to have significant implications on the maximum halo mass for quenching given the results in section 3.3. In that section, we found that the inward force is often dominated by gravity, while the outward force is dominated by supernova pressure. Both of these scale with fcoverf_{\rm cover} and therefore cancel in our maximum mass equation. However, our approximations actually break down in the regime where fcover≲0.1f_{\rm cover}\lesssim 0.1. The inclusion of an fcoverf_{\rm cover} factor in the force of gravity makes that force subdominant in many cases. When the accretion force is the dominant binding force, the maximum halo mass equation becomes

mh,max,fil\displaystyle m_{h,\rm max,fil} =1.9×1010M⊙(f∗0.01)3/2(κ0.035)−3/2(fcover0.01)3/2\displaystyle=1.9\times 10^{10}M_{\odot}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.035}\right)^{-3/2}\left(\frac{f_{\rm cover}}{0.01}\right)^{3/2} (36)
×{(tSF/tSN)2.31,if ​tSF≤tSN[(tSF−tSN)/tchar+1]3/2,if ​tSF>tSN,\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\left(t_{\rm SF}/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{2.31},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ [(t_{\rm SF}-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1]^{3/2},&\text{if }t_{\rm SF}>t_{\rm SN},\end{cases} (37)

which is significantly smaller than the isotropic case. Interestingly, because the force of gravity is subdominant in this form of the model, the equation is now dependent on the initial radius of the shell. If the star-forming region of the galaxies are larger than our fiducial κ=0.035\kappa=0.035 value by 10×10\times, then the maximum halo mass value decreases by 30×30\times. This result suggests that if filaments are present, then the star-forming region must be compact for mini-quenching to be effective.

4 Reproducing mini-quenching observables with our model

In this section, we expand our model to compare our results more rigorously with observations of mini-quenched galaxies and explore their implications for high-zz galaxy populations. For a fiducial model, we will assume a Chabrier-like IMF, f∗=0.01f_{*}=0.01, fcover=1f_{\rm cover}=1, κ=0.035\kappa=0.035, and set the maximum star formation time to tSF=100t_{\rm SF}=100 Myr.

There are three observable results we wish to reproduce with our model: the stellar masses of mini-quenched galaxies (m∗,totalm_{*,\rm total}), the quenching timescales (tquencht_{\rm quench}), and the amount of time mini-quenched galaxies were forming stars before they became mini-quenched (tSFt_{\rm SF}). Unfortunately, matching our model to stellar mass estimates is not a straightforward task, because there is not a single definition of “mini-quenched.” All of these quantities must also be extracted via SED fitting, so many have substantial uncertainties. Different authors apply the mini-quenching term to different populations Dome et al. (2024); Covelo-Paz et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2025); we therefore consider a broad mass range of m∗,total=107m_{*,\rm total}=10^{7}–1010​M⊙10^{10}M_{\odot}. The quenching timescale is similarly uncertain, if it is reported at all, though it is often found to be tquench∼10t_{\rm quench}\sim 10–2525 Myr. The timescale is unlikely to be many times larger than this, or galaxies with longer quenching timescales would have been observed (though their rapid fading in the rest-UV does make this challenging). We therefore expect quenching for ≲40\lesssim 40 Myr to be a reasonable target. We illustrate this expected range of values with the light green regions in the right column of figure 5.

We note that our model has several free parameters, while the observations of mini-quenched galaxies are so far limited to just a few examples. Thus our goal is not to develop a detailed set of constraints on the process but rather to examine the qualitative requirements set by mini-quenching in the context of our wind model.

4.1 Recreating mini-quenching stellar masses and quenching timescales

In figure 5, we show how our model compares to observations of mini-quenched galaxies at z=6z=6. In the top left panel, we plot the predicted quenching timescales for our model galaxies as a function of halo mass for several different SFEs. For reference, we plot the results of our equation 33 prediction as vertical dotted lines for each SFE value. Then, to convert these results to stellar mass, we scale the halo masses by m∗,total∼f~∗​(Ωb/Ωm)​mhm_{*,\rm total}\sim\tilde{f}_{*}(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h}, where f~∗\tilde{f}_{*} is the ratio of stellar mass to baryon mass. We plot each curve (except f∗=0.1f_{*}=0.1) with a range of f~∗=[0.01,0.1]\tilde{f}_{*}=[0.01,0.1], which matches the range of typical values in models Diemer and Kravtsov (2015); Furlanetto et al. (2017); Prada et al. (2026) and observations Finkelstein et al. (2015). In the top right panel, we find that our f∗=0.01f_{*}=0.01 curve can reproduce mini-quenching in nearly the entire range of masses and quenching timescales for our galaxies. In the same panel, we plot two example mini-quenched galaxies at z∼6z\sim 6. The first is JADES-GS-z7-01-QU Looser et al. (2024), whose stellar mass and quenching timescale values we quote from their fitting with bagpipes Carnall et al. (2018). (Note, however, that this galaxy is at z=7.3z=7.3; see figure 7 for the effect of redshift in our model). The second is MACS0417-z5BBG Strait et al. (2023), where we follow their quoted uncertainties. Our model can easily halt star formation in these galaxies for the required intervals, even at their relatively high stellar masses, indicating that kinetic feedback can be more effective than thermal injection Gelli et al. (2024).

These results suggest that mini-quenching in small galaxies (including those highlighted in the figure) is relatively easy to achieve, as long as the star formation efficiency is not too small, although more massive systems that have been discussed are much more difficult to explain (the green box in the figure). However, we note that, so long as supernova feedback is dominant, the star formation efficiency and the wind efficiency (ϵk\epsilon_{k}) are degenerate. We assume here (optimistically) that ϵk=1\epsilon_{k}=1, so that all of the supernova energy is available to drive the wind – if not, the requirements for mini-quenching becomes more stringent, requiring reasonably large star formation efficiencies. We also emphasize that we have assumed isotropic accretion in this figure; below we will find that filaments can also make the requirements much more stringent.

The ability to reproduce the stellar masses and quenching times also depends on the initial mass function in our model. In the bottom panels of figure 5, we show how different IMFs change the maximum halo mass that can be quenched. When we increase the characteristic turnover in the IMF to mchar=5​M⊙m_{\rm char}=5M_{\odot}, the increased feedback efficiency produces mini-quenching in nearly the entire stellar mass range of mini-quenched galaxies (bottom right panel), as expected from section 3.3.

We thus find that mini-quenching in moderately-massive galaxies can be achieved relatively easily. However, the timescales over which the quenching state can persist are very long for low-mass halos, which may conflict with observations.

4.2 Recreating star-formation timescales in mini-quenched galaxies

The third and last observable our model must reproduce is the duration of star formation before the onset of mini-quenching, which we have labeled tSFt_{\rm SF}.

Gelli et al. (2024) estimated tSFt_{\rm SF} for two galaxies by fitting their spectral energy distributions, assuming the galaxy star formation histories are well described as top-hat functions before the quenching period. They found tSF=30t_{\rm SF}=30 Myr (JADES-GS-z7-01-QU, Strait et al. (2023)) and tSF=40t_{\rm SF}=40 Myr (MACS0417-z5BBG, Looser et al. (2024)), although we note that other evidence points towards being cautious about inferring star-formation histories from quenched galaxies (e.g., Suess et al. (2022); Haskell et al. (2024); Narayanan et al. (2024)).

Our goal is to ensure our model can produce quenching quickly enough in galaxies with similar star-formation rate values as those observed. To do so, we return to the simplified model of section 3, but we use it to express the minimal requirements for mini-quenching in a different way: given a halo mass, we rearrange equation 33 to solve for the combination of f⋆f_{\star} and tSFt_{\rm SF} values that allow for mini-quenching. We then transform the SFE into the (observable) star formation rate, m˙∗\dot{m}_{*}, using equation 6. We show the results of this approach in figure 6, with various halo masses as dashed curves. We emphasize that these curves show the minimum star-formation rates that our model needs to have mini-quenching at those specific tSFt_{\rm SF} and mhm_{h} values. Another way to phrase this is that for a given halo mass curve, our model can create mini-quenching in halos up to that halo mass value. Mini-quenching can occur in halos with less mass for the associated m˙∗\dot{m}_{*} and tSFt_{\rm SF} values on the curve.

To compare our results with observations, we plot the two observed galaxies as stars in figure 6. We see that our fiducial model can cause mini-quenching in each of these galaxies if their halo masses are below the quoted values for the curves the observations lie on. To compare to the observations, however, we must convert these values to stellar masses. We find that the maximum halo mass calculated for MACS0417-z5BBG and JADES-GS-z7-01-QU match their quoted stellar mass values of f~∗∼0.02\tilde{f}_{*}\sim 0.02 and 0.030.03, respectively. Both of these values match model expectations Diemer and Kravtsov (2015); Furlanetto et al. (2017); Prada et al. (2026) and observations Finkelstein et al. (2015), so we conclude that our model can produce mini-quenching on fast enough timescales to match observations.

The curves in figure 6 are given for a constant halo mass, but for changing m˙∗\dot{m}_{*} values. Because the star-formation rate depends on both halo mass and f∗f_{*} (equation 6), movement along these curves corresponds to changing the star formation efficiency. Therefore, to guide the eye, we plot as dots two SFE values (f∗=0.01f_{*}=0.01 and f∗=0.001f_{*}=0.001). Both our example galaxies lie between these two values, suggesting that our model can create mini-quenching in galaxies with similar star-formation rates and tmaxt_{\rm max} values as those observed, if the example galaxies are within that range of star-formation efficiencies. We note that although f⋆f_{\star} is degenerate with the wind efficiency ϵk\epsilon_{k} in terms of the feedback efficiency, its effects are probably more subtle on this plot because the latter does not affect the star formation rate itself. However, to a first order, ϵk\epsilon_{k} still scales linearly with f∗f_{*}, and therefore if ϵk=0.1\epsilon_{k}=0.1 (rather than ϵk=1\epsilon_{k}=1, as assumed here), the required f∗f_{*} values in the plot would be 10×10\times larger.

We conclude that, with reasonable assumptions, mini-quenching following a star formation episode lasting ∼30\sim 30 Myr is relatively easy to achieve in our model. Thus, the key apparent challenge is understanding why the model predicts such long quenching timescales in small galaxies.

4.3 Quenching timescales at different redshifts

We have so far focused on mini-quenching at z∼6z\sim 6, but it has also been observed at redshifts lower than z∼6z\sim 6. For example, Merlin et al. (2025) observed many low-mass z∼3z\sim 3–55 galaxies that have been dormant for tquench≲150t_{\rm quench}\lesssim 150 Myr. There should also be mini-quenching at higher redshifts, but these galaxies are difficult to observe because the key observational quantity to confirm low star-formation rates (the Hα\alpha line) has redshifted out of detectability by z∼7.4z\sim 7.4 for many instruments Covelo-Paz et al. (2026).

Here, we explore how mini-quenching changes as a function of redshift. We must turn to our full numerical model to test the redshift dependence because assumptions in our simple analytic result break down at earlier times. For example, the accretion rate scales as m˙h∝(1+z)5/2\dot{m}_{h}\propto(1+z)^{5/2}, and Compton cooling, whose rate scales as tcomp∝(1+z)−4t_{\rm comp}\propto(1+z)^{-4}, becomes important at earlier times (see appendix B).

Figure 7 shows the quenching timescales of our model at a few different redshifts. Here the complex effects of redshift are apparent: the maximum mass of mini-quenched galaxies changes slightly from z=6z=6 to z=3z=3, though it changes drastically from z=6z=6 to z=9z=9. Lower redshifts produce longer quenching timescales as well. This result aligns with the trend that at z∼6z\sim 6, quenching timescales appear to be ≲40\lesssim 40 Myr, while at z∼3z\sim 3, these timescales have increased to ≲150\lesssim 150 Myr. While it is true that this lower-redshift sample could be contaminated with sources that are not mini-quenched but will be completely quenched (which can be the case even for low-mass early galaxies; see Baker et al. (2025a)), it is reassuring that the timescale that galaxies are mini-quenched at z=3z=3 is longer than the mini-quenching at z=6z=6.

4.4 The effects of filamentary accretion

A result of our model that should not be overlooked is that it predicts very long quenching timescales for many halo masses (see figure 5). Observations do allow tquench≳100t_{\rm quench}\gtrsim 100 Myr at z=6z=6, given that mini-quenched galaxies with longer timescales are likely more difficult to identify, so we may eventually observe some of them. However, the apparent discrepancy at low masses is large, so in this section, we explore how the inclusion of filaments (fcover<1f_{\rm cover}<1) affects the maximum quenching timescale.

Figure 8 shows the impact of the size of filaments on mini-quenching timescales. In this figure, we run our model for two values of f∗f_{*} (left and right panels) and with filaments of different sizes (parameterized by changing fcoverf_{\rm cover}). Recall that the accretion rate is held constant as we change fcoverf_{\rm cover}, so the primary effect of accretion is to increase the “momentum-loading” term in the wind propagation equation. The blue curves represent the model with isotropic accretion, or fcover=1f_{\rm cover}=1. When we decrease fcoverf_{\rm cover}, both the maximum halo mass and the quenching timescale drop dramatically. If we assume fcover=0.005f_{\rm cover}=0.005 (green line), as implied for all z=6z=6 observed galaxies by the model from Mandelker et al. (2018), mini-quenching becomes impossible. These results show the drastic effect filamentary accretion by gas has on mini-quenching in our model.

While filamentary accretion significantly decreases the maximum halo mass that is quenched in our model, it also decreases the quenching timescale. If fcover=0.1f_{\rm cover}=0.1, then the quenching timescale decreases from tquench>100t_{\rm quench}>100 Myr to tquench≲50t_{\rm quench}\lesssim 50 Myr in many cases. This change improves the agreement with observed systems because it increases the importance of accreting gas on the motion of the shell, which does not decrease with radius like gravity does.

Interestingly, we find that in the left panel of figure 8, a lower covering fraction can create a slightly larger quenching timescale for a range of halo masses. This effect is the result of the complicated interplay between the time spent forming stars and the quenching timescale. In a scenario with a smaller covering fraction, the galaxies spend more time forming stars before the galaxy becomes quenched, and in this range of halo masses, these extra stars result in longer quenched periods.

Thus, we find that narrow filamentary accretion has a dramatic effect on mini-quenching. Filaments as narrow as suggested by some models make it essentially impossible, because the incoming gas has such a high ram pressure. Mini-quenching can thus only occur if accretion at high redshifts occurs over extended filaments. That said, such filaments can decrease the timescale of quenching at low halo masses, alleviating one of the challenges of the model.

4.5 Sensitivity to initial conditions

We also plot in figure 8 as dashed blue curves the result of a model with fcover=1f_{\rm cover}=1 but initialized with 10%10\% of the initial gas mass. Such a setup might occur if a galaxy removed most of its gas in the previous quenching cycle. In this case, the quenching timescale decreases drastically. Therefore, another potential solution for the large quenching timescales at low halo masses is that these galaxies have already evacuated most of their gas in previous cycles. But such an occurrence also serves to decrease the star-formation rates of these galaxies, potentially causing disagreement in other observational quantities. For example, figure 6 displays the initial conditions that produce star-formation rates and tSFt_{\rm SF} which agree with observations. If we tweak the calculation so that the gas mass is 10%10\% of what we assumed in the figure, keeping all the other parameters constant, the required tSFt_{\rm SF} becomes ∼2\sim 2–3×3\times larger, disrupting the agreement with our model and the observations. Of course, we could compensate for this problem by adjusting other model parameters, such as by increasing the star-formation efficiency by 10×10\times or the halo mass by ∼4×\sim 4\times. These changes restore the agreement in figure 6, although these secondary changes have cascading effects (for example, by increasing the quenching timescales as well). Therefore, while initializing a galaxy with less interstellar gas is a solution to our too large quenching timescales at low masses, it does not appear to be a robust solution.

4.6 Estimating the fraction of galaxies in mini-quenched phases

So far, we have focused on mini-quenching in individual galaxies, but an interesting question is how common these systems are. A complete census of mini-quenched galaxies across the observed samples is currently very difficult, because of the challenges in identifying these systems and interpreting their spectra (though see Yang et al. (2025); Khullar et al. (2026)). On the theory side, simulations can be used, though they fail to reproduce all the characteristics of these galaxies in, e.g., the shape of quenched SEDs Gelli et al. (2023); Dome et al. (2024).

The fraction of time a galaxy is quenched (or its duty cycle) is fquench,i≈tquench/(tquench+tSF)f_{\mathrm{quench},i}\approx t_{\rm quench}/(t_{\rm quench}+t_{\rm SF}). This quantity can be folded together with the halo mass function to find the total fraction of galaxies that will be quenched at any given time:

fquench=∫log⁡mh,min∞fquench,i​(mh)​nh​(mh)​d​log⁡mh∫log⁡mh,min∞Φ⁡(mh)​d​log⁡mh,f_{\rm quench}=\frac{\int_{\log m_{h,\rm min}}^{\infty}f_{\mathrm{quench},i}(m_{h})n_{h}(m_{h})d\log m_{h}}{\int_{\log m_{h,\rm min}}^{\infty}\Phi(m_{h})d\log m_{h}}, (38)

where nhn_{h} is the halo mass function in units of number density per logarithmic interval of mass and mh,limm_{h,\rm lim} is the minimum halo mass observable by a survey. To compute this quantity, we use the Watson et al. (2013) halo mass function with the friends-of-friends halo-finding method Davis et al. (1985), though these choices will not significantly alter our results.

We use our full model to estimate this fraction in figure 9 (with a Chabrier-like IMF at z=6z=6). The first row assumes f∗=0.001f_{*}=0.001, while the second row takes f∗=0.01f_{*}=0.01. In each panel, we show three different cases for the accretion geometry, including isotropic accretion and filaments with different covering fractions. The second column takes the halo mass results in the first column and converts them to an approximate total stellar-mass range, assuming f~∗=[0.01,0.1]\tilde{f}_{*}=[0.01,0.1]. We find that a small fquenchf_{\rm quench} among low-mass galaxies only occurs if filaments are very narrow (fcover≪1f_{\rm cover}\ll 1).

Direct, observational tests for filaments at high redshift are impossible at the moment, though indirect tests might be possible. For example, our model predicts that galaxies accreting isotropically will be mini-quenched for much longer periods than galaxies accreting by gas filaments. Therefore, our model predicts that field galaxies may be mini-quenched for longer periods than galaxies in the Cosmic Web, if one makes the reasonable assumption that field galaxies accrete more isotropically than galaxies embedded in the Cosmic Web (which accrete by filaments). Simulations could test this prediction as well, though the simulation would have to span cosmological scales to securely estimate fquenchf_{\rm quench}, while still having a sufficiently high resolution to resolve outflows. Certainly, future work is required, and within our current capabilities.

5 Discussion

Our model is by construction quite simple. Here we consider a few well-motivated extensions that could help explain other observable features of the interactions of winds and accretion in mini-quenching.

5.1 Instabilities in the expanding shell

So far, we have assumed that mini-quenching continues until the feedback-driven shell stalls and falls back. However, it is very likely that these shells are actually part of complex multiphase media which impact the equally complex and multiphase CGM surrounding their host galaxies, including accreting streams. The complex flows can trigger instabilities in the wind, potentially allowing some fraction of the accreting material to penetrate the shell and resume star formation.

Here, we estimate the timescale over which one such instability may develop to be a limiting factor of the duration of mini-quenching episodes. We suppose the shell and the accreting gas experience Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities, as the low-density wind material collides with the surrounding CGM inside the halo gravitational potential well. This instability develops over a timescale τRT≡2​π/ω\tau_{\rm RT}\equiv 2\pi/\omega Mo et al. (2010), where ω=[gk(δ/(2+δ)]1/2\omega=[gk(\delta/(2+\delta)]^{1/2} is the linear growth rate of the instability and δ=1−ρsh/ρacc\delta=1-\rho_{\rm sh}/\rho_{\rm acc} is the overdensity of the shell relative to the accreting material. In this case, gg is the gravitational acceleration at the boundary of the two mediums and k=2​π/rk=2\pi/r is the wave number of the growing perturbation.

With r≈R0=κin​rvirr\approx R_{0}=\kappa_{\rm in}r_{\rm vir} being the initial radius of our shell and the gravitational acceleration being g=2​G​mh/κ​rvir2g=2Gm_{h}/\kappa r_{\rm vir}^{2}, the timescale for instabilities to grow is

τRT=2​πω=32Myr(δ2+δ)−1/2(κin0.07)(1+z7)−3/2,\tau_{\rm RT}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=32\ \mathrm{Myr}\left(\frac{\delta}{2+\delta}\right)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\kappa_{\rm in}}{0.07}\right)\left(\frac{1+z}{7}\right)^{-3/2}, (39)

where we have chosen κin\kappa_{\rm in} to be twice the fiducial starting shell value. If the accreting material is a few times denser than the shell (as is the case for strongly shocked material), δ∼3/4\delta\sim 3/4 and τRT∼60\tau_{\rm RT}\sim 60 Myr. At z=3z=3, τRT∼140\tau_{\rm RT}\sim 140 Myr. This is only a very rough estimate for the instability timescale (and others, such as the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, may also be relevant). Nevertheless, it is intriguing that these instability timescales roughly match estimates of the quenching timescales at both z∼6z\sim 6 and z∼3z\sim 3 (e.g., Covelo-Paz et al. (2026); Merlin et al. (2025)), suggesting that instabilities can help limit the extremely long quenching periods predicted by our model for small galaxies.

If we perform a similar process as section 4.6, a ceiling of tquench=30t_{\rm quench}=30 Myr decreases the quenching fraction by only ∼20%\sim 20\% up until mh,lim∼1011​M⊙m_{h,\rm lim}\sim 10^{11}M_{\odot}. At higher masses, the average quenching timescale of galaxies is already below 30 Myr, and the quenching fraction is unaffected. This result suggests that instabilities are an important part of mini-quenching, and understanding the dynamics of outflows is important in connecting the incidence of mini-quenching to theory models.

5.2 Can AGNs increase mini-quenching?

To this point, we have only considered stellar feedback, but an accretion episode could also trigger an AGN. In this section, we consider how AGN feedback may contribute to mini-quenching. This question is particularly interesting if the observed early galaxies accrete through thin filaments, for which supernova winds are far less effective. To explore this possibility, we use a simple analytic estimate similar to that of section 3. We begin by assuming that the black hole is accreting at the Eddington luminosity, LeddL_{\rm edd}, and that a fraction of the luminosity produced by the black hole provides feedback, ϵF\epsilon_{\rm F}. In this case, the feedback force produced by the black hole is FBH=fcover​ϵF​Ledd/cF_{\rm BH}=f_{\rm cover}\epsilon_{\rm F}L_{\rm edd}/c.33 3 Here we have assumed that the black hole feedback is itself isotropic. In most models of AGN feedback, winds and jets are not isotropic, but in that case they would only help with mini-quenching if the feedback and accretion flows were aligned. We ignore this possibility for simplicity. If the black hole is the only source of feedback and the force of accretion is much greater than the force of gravity (section 3.4), the galaxy is quenched if

fcover​ϵF​Leddc−d​mshd​t​vvir>0.f_{\rm cover}\epsilon_{\rm F}\frac{L_{\rm edd}}{c}-\frac{dm_{\rm sh}}{dt}v_{\rm vir}>0. (40)

The Eddington luminosity is Ledd=4​π​G​c​mp​mBH/σT∼1.3×1046​[erg/s]​(mBH/108​M⊙)L_{\rm edd}=4\pi Gcm_{p}m_{\rm BH}/\sigma_{\rm T}\sim 1.3\times 10^{46}\mathrm{[erg/s]}(m_{\rm BH}/10^{8}M_{\odot}), where mpm_{p} is the mass of the proton and σT\sigma_{\rm T} is the Thomson cross section. If the halo mass of the galaxy relates to the total stellar mass by mh=m∗,tot​(Ωm/Ωb)/f~∗m_{h}=m_{*,\rm tot}(\Omega_{m}/\Omega_{b})/\tilde{f}_{*}, the equation above can be used to estimate the largest stellar mass a galaxy can have to be mini-quenched:

m∗,tot,AGN≈2.5×107​M⊙​fcover3​ϵF3​(mBH/m∗,tot0.01)3​(f~∗0.1)4.m_{*,\rm tot,AGN}\approx 2.5\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot}\ f_{\rm cover}^{3}\epsilon_{\rm F}^{3}\left(\frac{m_{\rm BH}/m_{*,\rm tot}}{0.01}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{\tilde{f}_{*}}{0.1}\right)^{4}. (41)

Here we chosen a black-hole mass to stellar mass ratio of mBH/m∗,tot=0.01m_{\rm BH}/m_{*,\rm tot}=0.01, which agrees with observations of early black holes Harikane et al. (2023); Pacucci et al. (2023); Juodžbalis et al. (2025), but is large compared to local galaxies. Comparison to figure 5 shows that AGNs are somewhat less efficient than stellar feedback, which is not surprising on energetic grounds – while black hole accretion is about an order of magnitude more efficient than stellar fusion, the black holes are still much smaller than the host galaxies in our fiducial scaling.

The steep scaling with fcoverf_{\rm cover} implies that the additional AGN feedback still would not be enough to trigger mini-quenching if fcover∼0.005f_{\rm cover}\sim 0.005, as suggested by the analytic model of Mandelker et al. (2018). Our model therefore suggests that mini-quenched galaxies have relatively diffuse accretion channels.

5.3 Escaping winds and metal enrichment

One of the most widely-recognized implications of stellar feedback is large-scale chemical enrichment of the early Universe. Estimates of wind enrichment using feedback models similar to our own – with the important exception of ignoring the accretion flows and hence allowing continuous star formation – have shown that a substantial fraction of the IGM can be enriched by metals in this way (e.g., Ferrara et al. (2000); Madau et al. (2001); Furlanetto and Loeb (2003); Yamaguchi et al. (2023)). In contrast, in our model only the smallest halos are able to liberate the gas from the halo.

As noted, the key difference is in our treatment of accretion flows. Once mini-quenching occurs, and the initial wave of supernovae cease, the inward momentum added by accretion will inevitably stall the shell in all but the smallest systems. To estimate the maximum halo mass whose wind can escape the system (in isotropic accretion), the binding energy required to move a shell to the virial radius can be approximated as Eb=Eg+EaccE_{b}=E_{g}+E_{\rm acc}. We have seen that gravity dominates the inward force for r≲0.32​rvirr\lesssim 0.32r_{\rm vir}, and accretion dominates outside of that radius. Thus, we can estimate the energy required as the work to overcome the gravitational force to 0.32​rvir0.32r_{\rm vir} and the work to overcome the accretion force at larger radii. The energy pushing against the shell is at maximum the total energy from supernova, Einput=ϵSN​NSN×1051E_{\rm input}=\epsilon_{\rm SN}N_{\rm SN}\times 10^{51}erg (see appendix A for an analytic calculation of NSNN_{\rm SN}). If we set the binding energy equal to the input energy, we find the maximum halo mass that gas can escape an isotropically-accreting galaxy is

mh≲1×1011​M⊙​(f∗0.01)3/2,m_{h}\lesssim 1\times 10^{11}M_{\odot}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)^{3/2}, (42)

assuming a z=6z=6 galaxy forming stars for tSF=100t_{\rm SF}=100 Myr with a Chabrier-like IMF, and ϵSN=1\epsilon_{\rm SN}=1. Therefore, observed mini-quenched systems can remove gas from a galaxy, even in the presence of an accretion force. However, if the accreting gas has the same velocity outside the virial radius as it does inside it, the gas will eventually recycle back into the galaxy because the accretion force will continue to push on the outflowing gas outside the halo.

In the case of filaments, much of the gas will not encounter an accretion force because it is not incident on the accreting filaments. The outflowing gas will be subject only to the gravitational force and thus have an easier time leaving the galaxy. The maximum halo mass where the gas can escape the galaxy becomes mh≲1.5×1011​M⊙​(f∗/0.01)3/2m_{h}\lesssim 1.5\times 10^{11}M_{\odot}(f_{*}/0.01)^{3/2}, which is not a sizable difference. Further, this maximum halo mass resembles the values found in Furlanetto and Loeb (2003), which used a similar wind model, albeit without including the accretion force we have highlighted here.

5.4 Starbursts following a mini-quenching episode

We now consider another consequence of mini-quenching, relevant for any case in which the shell gas remains bound to the system. When a galaxy is mini-quenched, feedback from the galaxy (of any form) depletes the gas from the galaxy and prevents any further gas from accreting for the remainder of its quenching period. Afterwards, the galaxy begins to accrete again. But what happens to the gas that has been prevented from accreting onto the galaxy?

In the previous section, we showed that when accretion is included, mini-quenching can only temporarily prevent gas from falling back onto a galaxy, except at the smallest masses. Using the galaxy growth model in section 2.2, the amount of gas that will accrete over a quenching period, tquencht_{\rm quench}, is

Δ​macc=mg,i​(1−exp⁡[A​tquench​(1+z)5/2]),\Delta m_{\rm acc}=m_{g,i}(1-\exp[At_{\rm quench}(1+z)^{5/2}]), (43)

where mg,im_{g,i} is the initial gas mass in the galaxy before mini-quenching. Thus mini-quenching for ∼50\sim 50 Myr will temporarily prevent a gas mass ≳0.2​(Ωb/Ωm)​mh\gtrsim 0.2(\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m})m_{h} from accreting (or larger at z≫6z\gg 6) – which will then fall back quickly once the mini-quenching period ends, likely triggering another bout of rapid star formation.

Sun et al. (2026) found that early galaxies can form stars (at lower rates) out to ∼0.4​rv​i​r\sim 0.4r_{vir}. While their calculation is contextualized around star formation in a turbulent circumgalactic medium at early times, their results might apply to this scenario as well. Stars might form in the gas during infall, and there could be a large amount of star formation at once. However, a more sophisticated analysis will be required to determine the outcome of this large gas mass that will accrete post-quenching.

6 Conclusions

We have presented a model to explore how star formation can create mini-quenching in high-zz galaxies. Below, we lay out our key conclusions and their implications for mini-quenching.

We found that our model is able to reproduce key observables in mini-quenched galaxies with feedback from star formation. Galaxies in our model produce stellar feedback through a combination of dust-driven winds, radiation pressure by Lyα\alpha photons, and a pressure force created by supernova, with the last typically dominating. If these feedback forces overcome the binding forces of gravity and accretion (included explicitly in our model for the first time), the galaxy is quenched and the gas in the galaxy is pushed into a thin shell outside the star-forming region. The shell is expanded by feedback but eventually falls onto the galaxy again once star formation ceases and the feedback force fades. Using this model, we find:

  1. 1.

    Adopting plausible galaxy-formation parameter values (e.g., OPENf∗=0.01)f_{*}=0.01), supernovae provide enough feedback to remove gas from galaxies with similar stellar masses to observed mini-quenched galaxies at Cosmic Dawn – up to m∗,tot≈1010​M⊙m_{*,\rm tot}\approx 10^{10}M_{\odot} (figure 5), if accretion is isotropic rather than filamentary. This mass scale is sensitive to both the adopted star-formation efficiency (e.g., increasing f∗f_{*} by a factor of ten increases the mass scale by a factor of ∼15\sim 15) and the details of star formation (e.g., a top-heavy IMF can increase the threshold by up to ∼8×\sim 8\times).

  2. 2.

    Stellar feedback from a galaxy lasts long enough to reproduce the ≲50\lesssim 50 Myr quenching timescales of mini-quenched galaxies at z∼6z\sim 6 (figure 5). In fact, feedback in our model causes quenching for tquench≳100t_{\rm quench}\gtrsim 100 Myr with certain parameter choices, which is too long.

  3. 3.

    One possibility to reduce the quenching timescale is for the galaxy to accrete by filaments (figure 8). However, this is a balancing act, as filaments must be much larger than expected sizes from analytic models, or else the galaxy would not be able to prevent further accretion of cold gas and mini-quench the galaxy. A second solution is to appeal to instabilities in the expanding shell, which could prevent galaxies from being quenched for longer than ∼30\sim 30–100100 Myr. Such a solution also predicts that galaxies cannot be mini-quenched for long periods – in agreement with current (though biased) observations.

  4. 4.

    Supernovae provide energy at fast enough rates to mini-quench z=6z=6 galaxies with star-formation periods equal to or less than observed values (figure 6). If the observed star-formation timescales are correct, our model can mini-quench galaxies with a stellar mass to baryon mass ratio of ∼0.02\sim 0.02 – well within the range of expected and observed values.

  5. 5.

    Our model predicts that if galaxies accrete with thin filaments, then the fraction of galaxies that are mini-quenched is small. If a population of galaxies accretes isotropically (e.g., as field galaxies might), then their quenching timescales are long.

Future observations will be key to understand mini-quenched galaxies. Currently, our knowledge of the process is limited by the sparsity of observed systems. Upcoming surveys will no doubt reveal galaxies at all stages of quenching, helping us statistically measure the timescales associated with quenching, and therefore constraining the underlying galaxy formation parameters. Further, simulations capable of resolving the complicated dynamics of turbulent, interstellar gas at the edge of a galaxy, as well as the Cosmic Web as a whole, are forthcoming. Such simulations will illuminate the outer reaches of a galaxy, and advance our understanding of how outflowing gas interacts with accreting gas. In the future, we expect such improvements in understanding mini-quenching to provide a valuable window into early star formation.

Appendix A Analytic calculation of the number of supernova in our model

In this section, we calculate the number of supernovae that will occur after some time tt of star formation. We assume there has been no previous star formation, so that only the stars forming at t≥0t\geq 0 produce supernovae. In this calculation, we assume a Chabrier-like IMF (see section 2.4) and a galaxy at z=6z=6.

First, we will assume that stars have only been forming for t<tSNt<t_{\rm SN}, where tSN=55t_{\rm SN}=55 Myr (the lifetime of the smallest star to go supernova). At times longer than this, all the supernova will have gone off for the stars formed at t=0t=0 Myr. This adds complexity to the calculation, which we will expand upon later in this section.

We can calculate the rate of supernova occurring for a population of age Δ​t\Delta t using equation 15:

N˙​(Δ​t)=30​Myr−2​(f∗0.01)​(mh108​M⊙)​∫0Δ​td​t′​(t′Myr)−0.46,\dot{N}(\Delta t)=30\ \mathrm{Myr}^{-2}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)\int_{0}^{\Delta t}dt^{\prime}\left(\frac{t^{\prime}}{\rm Myr}\right)^{-0.46}, (44)

where we have assumed a constant halo mass for any given tmaxt_{\rm max} (though we include a factor to account for halo growth in equation 33). With this simplified equation, we compute a scaling relation for the rate of supernovae as a function of time and other parameters:

N˙​(Δ​t)=56​Myr−1​(Δ​tMyr)0.54​(f∗0.01)​(mh108​M⊙).\dot{N}(\Delta t)=56\ \mathrm{Myr}^{-1}\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\rm Myr}\right)^{0.54}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right). (45)

The total number of supernova to come after a time tt is achieved by integrating equation 45 such that

N⁡(t)=\displaystyle N(t)= ∫0tN˙​(t−t′)​d​t′\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\dot{N}(t-t^{\prime})dt^{\prime} (46)
=\displaystyle= 36​(tMyr)1.54​(f∗0.01)​(mh108​M⊙).\displaystyle\ 36\left(\frac{t}{\rm Myr}\right)^{1.54}\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right). (47)

Again, this expression holds for t<tSNt<t_{\rm SN}. If we wish to expand this calculation to t>55t>55 Myr, we have to recognize that for times t−t′>55t-t^{\prime}>55 Myr, all the supernovae generated by stars forming at a time t′t^{\prime} have exploded already. Thus for t>55t>55 Myr:

N⁡(t)=\displaystyle N(t)= ∫0tN˙​(t−t′)​d​t′\displaystyle\ \int_{0}^{t}\dot{N}(t-t^{\prime})dt^{\prime} (48)
=\displaystyle= N˙​(tSN)×(t−tSN)+∫0tSNN˙​(t−t′)​𝑑t\displaystyle\ \dot{N}(t_{\rm SN})\times(t-t_{\rm SN})+\int_{0}^{t_{\rm SN}}\dot{N}(t-t^{\prime})dt (49)
=\displaystyle= 488​(f∗0.01)​(mh108​M⊙)​(t−tSNMyr)+17237.\displaystyle\ 488\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)\left(\frac{t-t_{\rm SN}}{{\rm Myr}}\right)+17237. (50)

And therefore the final, generalized calculation for the number of supernova having occurred after time tt is

N⁡(t)=17237​(f∗0.01)​(mh108​M⊙)​{(t/tSN)1.54,if ​t≤tSN(t−tSN)/tchar+1,if ​t>tSN,N(t)=17237\left(\frac{f_{*}}{0.01}\right)\left(\frac{m_{h}}{10^{8}M_{\odot}}\right)\begin{cases}\left(t/t_{\rm SN}\right)^{1.54},&\text{if }t\leq t_{\rm SN}\\ (t-t_{\rm SN})/t_{\rm char}+1,&\text{if }t>t_{\rm SN},\end{cases} (51)

where tchar=36t_{\rm char}=36 Myr is a useful characteristic timescale to define.

Appendix B Effect of Compton cooling on the pressure from hot gas

In this section, we quantify the effects of Compton cooling by running our galaxy source model (section 2) for tSF=100t_{\rm SF}=100 Myr and track the luminosity output from supernova and from Compton cooling throughout.

In figure 10, we plot the ratio of supernova luminosity to the total luminosity impacting the pressure force for a number of parameters (though we take the absolute value of the luminosity of Compton cooling). In the left panel, we find that our approximation of zero Compton cooling is correct to ∼10%\sim 10\% if f∗≲0.01f_{*}\lesssim 0.01 and to ∼20%\sim 20\% at higher values of f∗f_{*}. We also find that the curves change slope at tSF∼55t_{\rm SF}\sim 55 Myr, which aligns with our timescale of tSN=55t_{\rm SN}=55 Myr (see appendix A). In the right panel of the figure, we plot the effect of Compton cooling for different redshifts. We find that at z=3z=3 and tSF=100t_{\rm SF}=100 Myr, Compton cooling provides a ∼1%\sim 1\% effect on the total pressure luminosity, though at z=9z=9, the Compton cooling quickly becomes important. Therefore, our approximations of zero Compton cooling in section 3 are accurate for z≲6z\lesssim 6.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
